Thanks for the product overview today. Procurement asked me to capture a couple of asks so we can move the contract forward:

- We need a clear definition of the monthly "safety net" — i.e., how monthly service credits are calculated when availability drops below the committed level.
- Echelon prefers a single, predictable monthly cap (as a percent of invoice) rather than a complicated banding matrix.
- We also need an explicit maintenance window definition and a carve-out for planned work.

High level: our legal/commercial team is comfortable with the concept of credits, but we want the cap, the uptime % and the math spelled out so finance can forecast risk.

Samir —

Thanks for the note and the SOW. Below is a concise framing you can share with finance/legal; happy to hop on a quick call to walk through the numbers.

Option A — Standard (recommended for general deployments):
- Target availability: 99.98% (monthly).
- Monthly remedy: service credits calculated as a percentage of that month’s invoice for the affected service.
- Cap: 10% of monthly bill.
- Maintenance: planned maintenance windows (standard) defined as up to 6 hours/month with 72-hour advance notice; outages during these windows are excluded.

Option B — Enterprise (for higher assurance):
- Target availability: 99.995% (monthly).
- Monthly remedy: same calculation method but smaller per-incident multipliers.
- Cap: 5% of monthly bill.
- Maintenance: 4 hours/month max and scheduled in coordination with Echelon; 7-day advance notice.

Operational safety net idea (to address your predictability ask):
- Remedy accounting uses a single-line calculation per month: (Committed uptime - Achieved uptime) * invoice_multiplier. That removes banding complexity.
- We can also provide an escrow option where a portion of monthly credits are pooled and settled quarterly for ease of forecasting.

I attached a redline (SLA_SafetyNet_Redline_v2.pdf) that lays out the single-line calculation and the two caps. If you prefer, we can propose Option A in the initial SOW and include a path to enterprise terms after a 3-month operational review.

Next steps: tell me whether finance prefers the predictable 10% cap or the tighter 5% enterprise option and I’ll get legal to bake the exact language and DocuSign flow.

Best,
Vanessa Ortiz
Director, Solutions — Redwood Inference
vanessa@redwoodinference.com

Vanessa / Ben —

Quick internal note on risk modeling if Echelon takes Option A (10% cap):
- For early-stage high-throughput customers we sometimes see month-to-month variance driven by traffic spikes and kernel-level degradations. A 10% cap is fine but we should protect via two operational controls in the contract:
  1) An explicit fallback policy: automatic routing to a cost-compatible model variant (not a full downgrade) after X minutes of degraded throughput.
  2) A 3-month operational review that can trigger re-tiering to Option B if usage patterns stabilize.

Also recommend we avoid a hard monthly maintenance allowance tied to a single number; instead allow for a rolling 90-day maintenance budget to avoid month-end surprises.

I can draft the internal risk paragraph for legal if you want to include it as an appendix.

—Marissa
